checklist.evidence: Use Yjs by default. Pick OT only if you want one authoritative server and don't need offline editing.
Document schema: the block types, text formatting and embeds a document can contain.
sending edits late, out of order and twice. Done when: thousands of random runs all end with identical copies.
Store periodic snapshots plus a log of every edit, and shrink the log from time to time.
Run several servers, routed by document ID or connected through Redis pub/sub. Slow down or limit clients that send too much.
Keep a local copy in the browser (IndexedDB), queue edits while offline, merge them on reconnect and show the connection status.
Enforce owner, editor, commenter and viewer roles on the server. Check every incoming edit against the schema, a size limit and a rate limit.
Undo should reverse only your own changes... A restore should be applied as a new edit, never by rewriting the edit log.
Show other people's cursors and selections and who's online, over a separate channel that isn't saved.
prove that edits made at the same time merge correctly before building anything on top
Targets: how many editors per document, maximum document size... Keep large documents fast.
If you change it later, you have to migrate every stored document.

traps.evidence: a CRDT (Yjs, Automerge) or OT/a central server that orders edits (ShareDB, prosemirror-collab)
Use Yjs by default... Keep the randomized merge tests anyway.
Single-user editor on the real schema. Every edit goes through the document model
Done when: restarting the server loses no edit the server had confirmed.
This is cheap with a CRDT and hard with OT.

note: An exceptionally sound, risk-first plan with accurate CRDT/OT reasoning, early convergence proof and checkable milestones; its weaknesses are absent cost analysis, thin deploy/rollback/versioning operations, and partial handling of live permission revocation and presence-cursor adjustment.
